title: Insert Interval
oneLinerQuestion: Insert a new interval into a sorted non-overlapping list and merge if necessary.
explanation:
Problem Intuition: The Insert Interval problem requires adding a new interval into an already sorted, non-overlapping list of intervals and merging any overlaps to preserve a non-overlapping, sorted result. Because the input list is already sorted by start time without mutual collisions, we do not need to re-sort from scratch in O(N log N) time. Instead, we can process the intervals in a single linear O(N) pass divided into three distinct chronological phases: strictly preceding intervals, overlapping intervals that merge into the new one, and strictly subsequent intervals.

- Step 1: Pre-Allocation & Loop Pointer Setup — We initialize an empty array 'result = []' to hold the modified interval sequence, and initialize a linear pointer 'i = 0' where N is the total length of the intervals array.

- Step 2: Phase 1 (Non-Overlapping Preceding Intervals) — While i < N and the current interval ends completely before the new interval starts (intervals[i][1] < newInterval[0]), there is zero possibility of overlap. We append intervals[i] directly into 'result' unchanged and advance 'i++'.

- Step 3: Phase 2 (Merging Overlapping Intervals) — While i < N and the current interval overlaps with the new interval (intervals[i][0] <= newInterval[1]), the ranges intersect. Instead of adding them immediately, we expand 'newInterval' to absorb the current interval: newInterval[0] = Math.min(newInterval[0], intervals[i][0]) and newInterval[1] = Math.max(newInterval[1], intervals[i][1]). We then advance 'i++' to check subsequent candidate intervals.

- Step 4: Phase 2 Placement — Once the overlapping condition breaks, 'newInterval' contains the fully merged boundary spanning all collisions. We append the unified 'newInterval' into 'result'.

- Step 5: Phase 3 (Non-Overlapping Subsequent Intervals) — While i < N, all remaining intervals start strictly after the newly merged interval ends (intervals[i][0] > newInterval[1]). We append each remaining intervals[i] directly into 'result' until the array is fully traversed.

- Step 6: Termination & Return — The 'result' array is returned, representing the complete set of ordered, disjoint intervals.

- Complexity & Memory Guarantees — Time Complexity: O(N) because each interval is evaluated and added to the output array exactly once in a single linear pass. Space Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space (excluding the output array) as the algorithm only uses index pointers and coordinate comparisons.
pseudoCode:
FUNCTION insert(intervals, newInterval):
    res = [], i = 0, n = LENGTH(intervals)
    WHILE i < n AND intervals[i].end < newInterval.start DO:
        APPEND intervals[i] TO res; i = i + 1
    END WHILE
    WHILE i < n AND intervals[i].start <= newInterval.end DO:
        newInterval.start = MIN(newInterval.start, intervals[i].start)
        newInterval.end = MAX(newInterval.end, intervals[i].end)
        i = i + 1
    END WHILE
    APPEND newInterval TO res
    WHILE i < n DO APPEND intervals[i] TO res; i = i + 1
    RETURN res
END FUNCTION
